entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11370"/><div sID="gen20570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11370"/><hi type="bold">3. righteous ... wicked--</hi>not contradictory of <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.4">Eze 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.9">9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23">Ge 18:23</reference>. Ezekiel here views the mere outward aspect of the indiscriminate universality of the national calamity. But really the same captivity to the "righteous" would prove a blessing as a wholesome discipline, which to the "wicked" would be an unmitigated punishment. The godly were sealed with a mark (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>), not for outward exemption from the common calamity, but as marked for the secret interpositions of Providence, overruling even evil to their good. The godly were by comparison so few, that not their salvation but the universality of the judgment is brought into view here. <div eID="gen20570" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11381"/><div sID="gen20592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11381"/>16. Apostrophe to the sword.<div eID="gen20592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20593" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go ... one way--</hi>or, "Concentrate thyself"; "Unite thy forces on the right hand" [Grotius]. The sword is commanded to take the nearest route for Jerusalem, "whither their face was set," whether south or north ("right hand or left"), according to where the several parts of the Chaldean host may be.<div eID="gen20593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or other, ... on the left--</hi>rather "set thyself on the left." The verbs are well-chosen. The main "concentration" of forces was to be on "the right hand," or south, the part of Judea in which Jerusalem was, and which lay south in marching from Babylon, whereas the Chaldean forces advancing on Jerusalem from Egypt, of which Jerusalem was north, were fewer, and therefore "set thyself" is the verb used. <div eID="gen20594" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11383"/><div sID="gen20597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11383"/><hi type="bold">19. two ways--</hi>The king coming from Babylon is represented in the graphic style of Ezekiel as reaching the point where the road branched off in two ways, one leading by the south, by Tadmor or Palmyra, to Rabbath of Ammon, east of Jordan; the other by the north, by Riblah in Syria, to Jerusalem--and hesitating which way to take. Ezekiel is told to "appoint the two ways" (as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.1">Eze 4:1</reference>); for Nebuchadnezzar, though knowing no other control but his own will and superstition, had really this path "appointed" for him by the all-ruling God.<div eID="gen20597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of one land--</hi>namely, Babylon.<div eID="gen20598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choose ... a place--</hi>literally, "a hand." So it is translated by Fairbairn, "make a finger-post," namely, at the head of the two ways, the hand post pointing Nebuchadnezzar to the way to Jerusalem as the way he should select. But Maurer rightly supports English Version. Ezekiel is told to "choose the place" where Nebuchadnezzar should do as is described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.20">Eze 21:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.21">21</reference>; so entirely does God order by the prophet every particular of place and time in the movements of the invader. <div eID="gen20599" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11390"/><div sID="gen20616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11390"/><hi type="bold">26. diadem--</hi>rather, "the miter" of the holy priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.4">Ex 28:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.5">Zec 3:5</reference>). His priestly emblem as representative of the priestly people. Both this and "the crown," the emblem of the kingdom, were to be removed, until they should be restored and united in the Mediator, Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>), [Fairbairn]. As, however, King Zedekiah alone, not the high priest also, is referred to in the context, English Version is supported by Gesenius.<div eID="gen20616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this shall not be the same--</hi>The diadem shall not be as it was [Rosenmuller]. Nothing shall remain what it was [Fairbairn].<div eID="gen20617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exalt ... low, ... abase ... high--</hi>not the general truth expressed (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">Pr 3:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.52">Lu 1:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jas 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference>); but specially referring to Messiah and Zedekiah contrasted together. The "tender plant ... out of the dry ground" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>) is to be "exalted" in the end (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>); the now "high" representative on David's throne, Zedekiah, is to be "abased." The outward relations of things shall be made to change places in just retaliation on the people for having so perverted the moral relations of things [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen20618" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11391"/><div sID="gen20619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11391"/>27. Literally, "An overturning, overturning, overturning, will I make it." The threefold repetition denotes the awful certainty of the event; not as Rosenmuller explains, the overthrow of the three, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah; for Zedekiah alone is referred to.<div eID="gen20619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is--</hi>strikingly parallel to <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>. Nowhere shall there be rest or permanence; all things shall be in fluctuation until He comes who, as the rightful Heir, shall restore the throne of David that fell with Zedekiah. The Hebrew for "right" is "judgment"; it perhaps includes, besides the right to rule, the idea of His rule being one in righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Re 19:11</reference>). Others (Nebuchadnezzar, &c.), who held the rule of the earth delegated to them by God, abused it by unrighteousness, and so forfeited the "right." He both has the truest "right" to the rule, and exercises it in "right." It is true the tribal "scepter" continued with Judah "till Shiloh came" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>); but there was no kingly scepter till Messiah came, as the spiritual King then (<reference osisRef="John.18.36">Joh 18:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.18.37">37</reference>); this spiritual kingdom being about to pass into the literal, personal kingdom over Israel at His second coming, when, and not before, this prophecy shall have its exhaustive fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.7">10:7</reference>; "To thee doth it appertain"). <div eID="gen20620" type="x-p"/>

Lest Ammon should think to escape because Nebuchadnezzar had taken the route to Jerusalem, Ezekiel denounces judgment against Ammon, without the prospect of a restoration such as awaited Israel. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">Jr 49:6</reference>, it is true, speaks of a "bringing again of its captivity," but this probably refers to its spiritual restoration under Messiah; or, if referring to it politically, must refer to but a partial restoration at the downfall of Babylon under Cyrus.<div eID="gen20621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their reproach--</hi>This constituted a leading feature in their guilt; they treated with proud contumely the covenant-people after the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">Eze 25:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.9">Zep 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>), and appropriated Israel's territory (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">Jr 49:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13-Amos.1.15">Am 1:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen20622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furbished, to consume--</hi>Maurer punctuates thus, "Drawn for the slaughter, it is furbished to devour ('consume'), to glitter." English Version, "to consume because of the glittering," means, "to consume by reason of the lightning, flash-like rapidity with which it falls." Five years after the fall of Jerusalem, Ammon was destroyed for aiding Ishmael in usurping the government of Judea against the will of the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.25">2Ki 25:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.15">Jr 41:15</reference>) [Grotius]. <div eID="gen20623" type="x-p"/>

Lest Ammon should think to escape because Nebuchadnezzar had taken the route to Jerusalem, Ezekiel denounces judgment against Ammon, without the prospect of a restoration such as awaited Israel. Jr 49:6 , it is true, speaks of a "bringing again of its captivity," but this probably refers to its spiritual restoration under Messiah; or, if referring to it politically, must refer to but a partial restoration at the downfall of Babylon under Cyrus. their reproach-- This constituted a leading feature in their guilt; they treated with proud contumely the covenant-people after the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar ( Eze 25:3 , 6 ; Zep 2:9 , 10 ), and appropriated Israel's territory ( Jr 49:1 ; Am 1:13-15 ). furbished, to consume-- Maurer punctuates thus, "Drawn for the slaughter, it is furbished to devour ('consume'), to glitter." English Version, "to consume because of the glittering," means, "to consume by reason of the lightning, flash-like rapidity with which it falls." Five years after the fall of Jerusalem, Ammon was destroyed for aiding Ishmael in usurping the government of Judea against the will of the king of Babylon ( 2Ki 25:25 ; Jr 41:15 ) [Grotius].
